title: D.B. Cooper: The Man Who Vanished

NARRATOR.desc: Documentary narrator: confident, brisk, dry wit, suspense on the reveals

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: November 24th, 1971. The day before Thanksgiving.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: A quiet man in a dark suit and a black clip-on tie walks up to the Northwest Orient counter in Portland, Oregon.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He pays cash for a one-way ticket to Seattle. A thirty-minute hop. The name he gives? Dan Cooper.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He takes seat 18E, the very last row, and orders a bourbon and soda.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Just after three p.m., he slips a note to a flight attendant. She assumes it's his phone number, and pockets it.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: It is not his phone number.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Miss, I have a bomb in my briefcase. I want you to sit by me.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He cracks open the case. Wires. Red sticks.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: His demands: $200,000 in twenty-dollar bills. And four parachutes.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Five hours later, somewhere over the black forests of southwest Washington, he lowers the rear stairs of a Boeing 727, and steps out into the night.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He was never seen again.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Fifty-five years. More than 800 suspects. 66 volumes of FBI files.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And still, nobody knows who this man really was.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Even the name the whole world remembers him by is wrong.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: His ticket said Dan Cooper. But early on, agents questioned a Portland man named D.B. Cooper, who had nothing to do with it, and a reporter on deadline ran with those initials.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: The wire services picked it up. And a mistake became a legend.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: So let's go back to row eighteen.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Schaffner rushes the note to the cockpit. The captain, William Scott, radios the airline, and the airline's president makes a fast decision: give the man whatever he wants.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Another flight attendant, Tina Mucklow, takes the seat beside him. For the next few hours, she is his messenger to the cockpit.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And Cooper? Calm. Polite. He even seems to know the area, pointing out Tacoma below, and noting that McChord Air Force Base is only twenty minutes from the airport.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: As the jet circles Puget Sound for about two hours, the ground below goes into overdrive.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Seattle First National Bank gathers ten thousand unmarked twenty-dollar bills. The FBI photographs every single one, recording the serial numbers on microfilm.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: The parachutes come from a local skydiving school, and a stunt pilot named Norman Hayden.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Cooper had turned down military parachutes. He wanted civilian ones, with ripcords he could pull himself. A small detail. A smart one.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Just before six, Flight 305 lands in Seattle. Cooper orders every window shade pulled down, to keep police snipers guessing. The money and the parachutes are brought aboard.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: In exchange, all thirty-five other passengers walk off the plane. Most of them never realized they had been hijacked.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Then he gives the crew his flight plan.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Mexico City. The slowest speed possible without stalling. Landing gear down. Wing flaps at fifteen degrees. No higher than ten thousand feet. Cabin unpressurized.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And one more thing: the rear airstair down. The airline said taking off like that was unsafe, so he agreed to lower it himself, once they were in the air.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Here's the key. The Boeing 727 had something almost no other airliner had: a staircase that opens under the tail. And it could be opened in flight. He knew that.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: At about seven forty p.m., the jet takes off into a cold, rainy night. Two F-106 fighter jets shadow it from a distance.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Cooper sends Tina Mucklow to the cockpit and tells her to stay there. She is the last person to see him.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Around eight o'clock, a warning light comes on in the cockpit. The airstair is open.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: At eight thirteen, the crew feels a sudden jolt. The tail pitches up. And then... nothing.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: They keep flying, all the way to Reno, Nevada, landing at eleven oh two p.m., with the stairs still hanging down.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Agents rush the cabin. It's empty. No Cooper. No money. Just two of the four parachutes, his clip-on tie, and eight cigarette butts.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: What followed was one of the longest investigations in FBI history. Codename: NORJAK. Northwest hijacking.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Agents calculated a likely jump zone near the small town of Ariel, Washington, close to Lake Merwin. Thick forest, steep hills, and in November, freezing rain.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Soldiers from Fort Lewis combed the woods for weeks. The Air Force even sent an SR-71 spy plane to photograph the flight path. It found nothing.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Within five years, the FBI had looked at more than 800 suspects.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And meanwhile, America had a new problem. Copycats.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: In 1972 alone, there were thirty-one hijackings in American airspace. Fifteen of those hijackers demanded parachutes.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Five months after Cooper, a former Green Beret named Richard McCoy hijacked a United jet, collected half a million dollars, and parachuted out over Utah. He was arrested two days later.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: So the rules changed. Every Boeing 727 was fitted with a simple spring-loaded latch that stops the rear stairs from opening in flight. It is still called the Cooper vane.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And from 1973, airlines had to search every passenger and every bag. That airport security line you stand in? You can partly thank Dan Cooper.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: For years, the trail went cold. Then, the forest started giving things back.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: In 1978, a deer hunter found a placard from a 727's rear airstair, about thirteen miles east of Castle Rock, Washington. Right under the flight path.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Then, on February 10th, 1980, an eight-year-old boy named Brian Ingram was on a family outing at Tena Bar, on the Columbia River.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Raking the sand for a campfire, he dug up three bundles of rotting twenty-dollar bills. Five thousand eight hundred dollars.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: The serial numbers matched. This was Cooper's money.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: It was the biggest break in the case. And the most confusing one.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Tena Bar is miles from the jump zone. So how did the money get there? Washed down a river? Moved by dredging? Buried on purpose? Nobody has ever agreed.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Brian was later allowed to keep some of the bills. In 2008, he sold fifteen of them at auction for about thirty-seven thousand dollars. Not a bad return on a twenty.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And the tie? Decades later, a team of researchers found something odd on it: tiny particles of titanium, and rare earth metals.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: In 1971, that kind of titanium was used in only a few places, like aerospace and chemical plants. Was Cooper an engineer? A plant worker? The tie can't say.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: So who was he? Over the decades, a few names keep coming back.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Richard McCoy, the copycat. Same method, same plane. But the FBI ruled him out. Wrong age, wrong eyes, and he didn't match the crew's descriptions. He was killed in a shootout with agents in 1974.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Robert Rackstraw, a Vietnam veteran and pilot with a criminal record. Investigators cleared him in 1979, but some researchers still insist it was him. He died in 2019.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Sheridan Peterson, a former smokejumper and Boeing technical editor. But a DNA comparison using the tie did not point to him.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Then, in 2024, a twist. McCoy's own children went public, saying their late father was Cooper, after a YouTuber found an old parachute rig on family property in North Carolina. The family says the FBI took it. The FBI has never publicly confirmed a thing.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Officially, the FBI suspended its active investigation in July 2016. But the files keep coming. Batch after batch of pages, released to the public, right up to today.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Many agents believe the simplest answer. He didn't survive. A night jump, in a business suit, in freezing rain, over thick forest.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: But if he died, where is he? No body. No parachute. No briefcase. In fifty-five years, not one trace of the man himself has ever turned up.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Maybe he hit the trees and was never found. Or maybe he walked out of that forest, buried his money, and went home for Thanksgiving.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: The only certain thing is this. On a rainy night in 1971, a man in a J.C. Penney clip-on tie stepped off the back of a jet with $200,000, and stepped straight into history.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: His real name is still out there. Somewhere.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: This was Ink and Antiquity. If you have a theory, leave it in the comments. And subscribe, because history has plenty more mysteries like this one.
